agree.reason: The nurse's log, the survey and the nearby district's results make a strong case for an undecided reader. A board member worried about the $180,000 or the athletic director's concerns gets mostly argument and promises rather than answers, so that reader is less likely to be persuaded.

honest.reason: The piece wisely avoids promising that graduation rates will rise, but it states things the facts don't support: it says first period is "the class they miss most" with no attendance data from this school, it adds the 11 p.m. sleep science, and it calls the change "the cheapest place" to start despite the $180,000 cost.

works_the_facts.reason: It correctly shows that first-period visits (412) outnumber second and third combined (369), and it turns 640/890 into "nearly three in four" and 84% into "one in six". It never puts the $180,000 per student or against the cost of repeated classes, so the bus cost is never actually weighed.

right_comparison.reason: The status quo is described honestly through the daily first-period cost, and the nearby district serves as a real-world comparison. However, there's no trend data, and "what we already pay" for tired students is asserted, not shown.

qualification.reason: The vote-yes-then-measure plan names checkable measures (nurse visits, tardies, attendance, course failures) and a one-year review date. It sets no target number, and the only consequence of a miss is "I'll be the first to say so."

objections.reason: All three objections are taken up fairly. The answers on working parents and athletics are concrete, but the early-open plan adds a staffing cost it doesn't mention, and the bus answer is thin.

fit.reason: It has the right op-ed form with a headline, byline and bio line, but at roughly 700 words it runs past the 650-word limit.
